solution.text:
3. Superconducting mesh
Trapped flux and two images
Superconductivity locks the local flux through the small mesh holes. The normal field on the plane retains the value it had when the dipole was at \(a\). Put the mesh at \(z=0\), the real dipole at \(z=b>0\), and take positive force away from the mesh. Two image dipoles reproduce that boundary condition: an image at \(z=-a\) with the original orientation and moment, plus an image at \(z=-b\) with opposite moment. The first preserves the original normal field, and the second cancels the real dipole's new normal field. For \(b=a\), the images cancel, as required.
Dipole force
Model a dipole temporarily as poles \(q_m\) and \(-q_m\) a distance \(d\) apart, so \(m=q_md\). Its axial field at a large distance \(x\) is
\[B(x)=\frac{\mu_0q_m}{4\pi}\left[\frac1{x^2}-\frac1{(x+d)^2}\right]\simeq\frac{\mu_0m}{2\pi x^3}.\]
The force between parallel coaxial dipoles follows from the field gradient, with magnitude \(3\mu_0m^2/(2\pi x^4)\), directed attractively. Antiparallel dipoles repel. Adding the two image forces yields
\[F_z=-\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{2\pi(a+b)^4}+\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{2\pi(2b)^4}=\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{2\pi}\left[\frac1{16b^4}-\frac1{(a+b)^4}\right].\]
Negative \(F_z\) means attraction towards the mesh. No factor of one half multiplies the force: it is the actual field at the real dipole due to the induced currents.
Small displacement check
\[b=a+\delta,\quad |\delta|\ll a:\qquad F_z\simeq-\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{16\pi a^5}\delta.\]
The force restores the initial position, giving small harmonic oscillations if the dipole is free to move in this direction. The original partial-credit rules remain in the solution PDF.
